claims.source: Although the magnitude of these subdomain rotations in the leading head are smaller than was measured in prior studies with monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, the orientation of the rotation axes are approximately consistent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,F) (Cao et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous studies, with citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The subdomain rotations will close the docking cleft and sterically obstruct neck linker docking in the leading head.
claims.source: Functionally these rotations will close the docking cleft and sterically obstruct neck linker docking in the leading head.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the observed rotations.

claims.claim: The observations are consistent with an 'alternating cleft' model, which posits that the trailing head will have a closed nucleotide cleft and an open docking cleft, while the leading head will have an open nucleotide cleft with reduced affinity for nucleotides and a closed docking cleft that precludes neck linker docking.
claims.source: The above observations are consistent with an 'alternating cleft' model, proposed based on prior studies of monomeric kinesins, which posits that the trailing head of a kinesin dimer will have a closed nucleotide cleft and an open docking cleft, while the leading head will have the opposite (an open nucleotide cleft with reduced affinity for nucleotides and a closed docking cleft that precludes neck linker docking) (Shang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the consistency with a proposed model, with citations to Shang et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The current work provides direct support for the alternating cleft model by visualizing the conformations of the clefts in dimeric kinesin.
claims.source: The current work provides direct support for this model by visualizing the conformations of the clefts in dimeric kinesin.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the current findings.

claims.claim: The trailing head may be well modeled by structures of monomeric kinesins co-complexed with ATP analogs.
claims.source: The above features of the trailing head, including a closed nucleotide cleft and a docked neck linker, indicate that this head may be well modeled by structures of monomeric kinesins co-complexed with ATP analogs (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about structural similarity, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The leading head shares certain features with structures of monomeric kinesins in the no-nucleotide state, including an open nucleotide cleft with disordered switch I loop and a closed docking cleft.
claims.source: On the other hand, the leading head shares certain features with structures of monomeric kinesins in the no-nucleotide state, including an open nucleotide cleft with disordered switch I loop and a closed docking cleft (Cao et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about structural similarity, with citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the no-nucleotide state (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively).
claims.source: In line with the above analysis, the trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin (EMDB: 6187) more closely than the no-nucleotide state (EMDB: 6188) (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively), and the leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cross-correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
claims.source: In line with the above analysis, the trailing heads resemble the ATP-like state of monomeric kinesin (EMDB: 6187) more closely than the no-nucleotide state (EMDB: 6188) (cross-correlation scores were 0.73–0.74 and 0.67, respectively), and the leading heads resemble the no-nucleotide state of monomeric kinesin more closely than the ATP-like state (cross-correlation scores: 0.77–0.78 versus 0.69, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cross-correlation analysis.

claims.claim: These correlation scores are consistent with the 'alternating cleft' model.
claims.source: These correlation scores are consistent with the 'alternating cleft' model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the consistency with the model.

claims.claim: Reconstruction of '010' sites identified kinesin dimers that attach to microtubules with only one head, termed singly-bound heads.
claims.source: In order to address this question, we searched for isolated motor domains with no neighboring head along the same protofilament ('010' pattern in the kinesin-binding matrices). Reconstruction of these sites identified kinesin dimers that attach to microtubules with only one head, which are termed singly-bound heads (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: The absence of enriched kinesin density at diagonally adjacent sites indicates that non-canonical stepping configurations are unlikely in the sample.
claims.source: While in principle these '010' sites could reflect non-canonical stepping configurations, in which the partner head has stepped diagonally onto an adjacent protofilament, the absence of enriched kinesin density at diagonally adjacent sites indicates that this possibility is unlikely in our sample (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the absence of expected density.

claims.claim: The singly-bound head adopts a closed conformation of the nucleotide cleft.
claims.source: Because detachment of the partner head removes stereochemical constraints, under our experimental conditions, a singly-bound head might be expected to assume an ATP-like state as previously observed in monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, including nucleotide binding, an ordered switch I loop and a docked neck linker (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014). We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The singly-bound head has an ordered switch I loop.
claims.source: Because detachment of the partner head removes stereochemical constraints, under our experimental conditions, a singly-bound head might be expected to assume an ATP-like state as previously observed in monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, including nucleotide binding, an ordered switch I loop and a docked neck linker (Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014). We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citations to Gigant et al., 2013 and Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains in the singly-bound head are indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of the dimer maps.
claims.source: We observed the first two features in the singly-bound head (Figure 5B); moreover, when we quantified the orientations of the switch I/II and P-loop subdomains, they were indistinguishable from those seen in the trailing head of our dimer maps (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: Density for the neck linker in the singly-bound head is not evident.
claims.source: However, density for the neck linker in the singly-bound head is not evident and continuous density is observed between helix α6 and the microtubule surface, similar to the leading head (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: There is no trace of density for the coiled coil in the singly-bound head map.
claims.source: Moreover, there is no trace of density for the coiled coil in this map (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: The singly-bound head represents a novel conformation of kinesin that is mainly ATP-like but with a disordered neck linker.
claims.source: Thus, the singly-bound head appears to represent a novel conformation of kinesin that is mainly ATP-like but with a disordered neck linker.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the structural features observed.

claims.claim: The trailing and leading heads in the kinesin dimer map closely resemble previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins in ATP-like and no-nucleotide states, respectively.
claims.source: As we have shown, the trailing and leading heads in our kinesin dimer map closely resemble previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins in ATP-like and no-nucleotide states, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claims.claim: The mechanistic causes of the conformational differences between the two heads of a dimer in the current work and between the two nucleotide states of monomeric kinesin are not the same.
claims.source: However, it is important to note that the underlying mechanistic causes of the conformational differences between the two heads of a dimer in the current work and between the two nucleotide states of monomeric kinesin are not the same.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the mechanistic differences.

claims.claim: In previous studies with monomeric kinesin, the motor domains were locked into a certain conformation by the nucleotide conditions used in the experiments.
claims.source: In previous studies with monomeric kinesin, the motor domains were locked into a certain conformation by the nucleotide conditions used in the experiments. More specifically, AlFx was used to lock the motor domain in an ATP-like state (ADP•AlFx), or apyrase was used to remove all nucleotides to ensure a no-nucleotide state (Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a description of previous experimental approaches, with citations to Cao et al., 2014; Gigant et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The two heads in the dimer sample are biochemically identical and are exposed to the same level of ATP and AlFx in the environment, yet they exhibit different conformations and different levels of nucleotide binding.
claims.source: In contrast, the two heads in our dimer sample are biochemically identical and are exposed to the same level of ATP and AlFx in the environment, and yet strikingly they exhibit different conformations and different levels of nucleotide binding.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The different orientations of the neck linkers that connect the two heads explain the different conformations and nucleotide binding levels of the two heads.
claims.source: The only logical explanation for this observation lies in the different orientations of the neck linkers that connect the two heads, since all other factors appear identical in our experimental conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The alternating cleft model provides a structural explanation for the different conformations of the two heads in the dimer.
claims.source: The alternating cleft model provides a structural explanation for understanding this behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the explanatory power of the model.

claims.claim: Due to inter-head geometric constraints, the neck linker in the leading head must orient rearward to connect with the trailing head.
claims.source: Due to inter-head geometric constraints, the neck linker in the leading head must orient rearward to connect with the trailing head.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the geometric constraints.

claims.claim: The rearward orientation of the neck linker prevents neck linker docking in the leading head and thus favors a closed docking cleft, leading to a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain that opens up the nucleotide cleft concomitantly.
claims.source: As a result of this rearward orientation, neck linker docking cannot be achieved in the leading head and thus a closed docking cleft will be favored, leading to a seesaw-like rotation of the P-loop subdomain that opens up the nucleotide cleft concomitantly.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the structural consequences of the rearward orientation.

claims.claim: The current results directly visualize evidence of the coupling between the docking cleft and the nucleotide cleft due to rearwards pulling of the neck linker.
claims.source: We have now directly visualized evidence of this coupling between the docking cleft and the nucleotide cleft due to rearwards pulling of the neck linker.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the structural findings.

claims.claim: The results tend to disfavor a competing 'water cap' model that involves melting of the C-terminus of the switch II helix and other structural features that are not observed in the current dimer map.
claims.source: Our results therefore tend to disfavor a competing 'water cap' model (Morikawa et al., 2015; Nitta et al., 2008) that involves melting of the C-terminus of the switch II helix and other structural features that are not observed in the current dimer map.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the implications for competing models, with citations to Morikawa et al., 2015 and Nitta et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Density corresponding to the nucleotide can still be observed in the leading head, albeit weaker compared to the trailing head.
claims.source: We observed several significant discrepancies between the kinesin dimer map and previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins that underlie the alternating cleft model (Shang et al., 2014). First, density corresponding to the nucleotide can still be observed in the leading head (albeit weaker compared to the trailing head), contrasting with the general expectation that nucleotide binding in the leading head should be strongly disfavored in the two-head-bound state.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, with citation to Shang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The magnitude of rotation of the P-loop subdomain is not as large in the leading head as in monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, although the orientations of the rotation axes are approximately consistent.
claims.source: Second, the magnitude of rotation of the P-loop subdomain is not as large in the leading head as in monomeric kinesin in the no-nucleotide state, although the orientations of the rotation axes are approximately consistent.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: ATP may still bind in the leading head to some extent, albeit with reduced affinity, in which case the leading head density will reflect a mixture of ATP-bound and -unbound states.
claims.source: These discrepancies could indicate that ATP still binds in the leading head to some extent, albeit with reduced affinity, in which case our leading head density will reflect a mixture of ATP-bound and -unbound states.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the discrepancies.

claims.claim: No published work can solidly rule out the possibility that ATP still binds in the leading head to some extent.
claims.source: To the best of our knowledge, no published work can solidly rule out this possibility (Asenjo et al., 2003; Isojima et al., 2016; Mickolajczyk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, with citations to Asenjo et al., 2003; Isojima et al., 2016; Mickolajczyk et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The discrepancies may arise from a contamination artifact due to incomplete sorting of kinesin dimers by FINDKIN.
claims.source: An alternative explanation for the above discrepancies is that they arise from a contamination artifact, i.e. due to incomplete sorting of kinesin dimers by FINDKIN.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation.

claims.claim: The presence of singly-bound heads in the dataset introduces the possibility that two singly-bound heads may occupy adjacent sites along one protofilament, a configuration FINDKIN will falsely identify as a doubly-attached dimer.
claims.source: Due to its design, the FINDKIN algorithm is highly effective at aligning and reconstructing kinesin dimers if they all exist in a two-head-bound state. However, the presence of singly-bound heads in our dataset (where the partner head is detached from the microtubules) introduces the possibility that two singly-bound heads may occupy adjacent sites along one protofilament, a configuration FINDKIN will falsely identify as a doubly-attached dimer.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about a potential source of error in the method.

claims.claim: Densities of both leading and trailing heads in the dimer map are expected to be 'contaminated' through mixing with the singly-bound heads.
claims.source: We therefore expect that densities of both leading and trailing heads in our map will be 'contaminated' through mixing with the singly-bound heads.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the expected consequence of the error.

claims.claim: A model of a 'contaminated' leading head generated by averaging the monomeric kinesin density map in the no-nucleotide state and the singly-bound head displays increased nucleotide density and a smaller rotation of the P-loop subdomain.
claims.source: In order to test whether features in the leading head density may be explained by such a contamination artifact, we generated a model of a 'contaminated' leading head by averaging the monomeric kinesin density map in the no-nucleotide state and the singly-bound head, and this mixture model displays increased nucleotide density and a smaller rotation of the P-loop subdomain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The trailing head differs from monomeric kinesin in the ATP-like state in that its neck linker density is weaker, which may be explained by contamination with the singly-bound head.
claims.source: Moreover, the trailing head also differs from monomeric kinesin in the ATP-like state in that its neck linker density is weaker. This latter effect may also be explained by contamination with the singly-bound head, which exhibits no neck linker density.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about a possible explanation for the observed difference.

claims.claim: The contamination artifact could help explain why cross-correlation scores comparing motor domains from the dimer maps with each other are substantially higher than scores comparing dimeric motor domains with monomeric ones.
claims.source: The presence of such 'contamination' could also help explain why cross-correlation scores that compare motor domains from our dimer maps with each other (ranging from 0.86 to 0.92; see Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) are substantially higher than scores that compare dimeric motor domains with monomeric ones (ranging from 0.67 to 0.78; see Figure 4—figure supplement 3A): by causing trailing and leading heads to be averaged with a common structure (the singly-bound head), the contamination artifact would tend to artificially increase the similarity of the leading and trailing heads in our dimer maps.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the impact of contamination on cross-correlation scores.

claims.claim: At least some of the discrepancies between the dimer map and the previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins can be attributed to 'contamination' with the singly-bound heads.
claims.source: It therefore appears likely that at least some of the discrepancies between our dimer map and the previously determined structures of monomeric kinesins can be attributed to 'contamination' with the singly-bound heads.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the likely explanation for the discrepancies.

claims.claim: The possibility of ATP binding in the lead head is not mutually exclusive with the contamination artifact.
claims.source: The other proposed explanation (ATP binding in the lead head), however, is not mutually exclusive with this contamination artifact, and there appears to be no clear indication from published work that either one is more probable.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between two possible explanations.

claims.claim: Further experiments are required to characterize key properties of the leading head, including the kinetics/affinity of ATP binding as well as the effects of ATP binding on the conformation of the nucleotide cleft.
claims.source: Further experiments are required to characterize key properties of the leading head, including the kinetics/affinity of ATP binding as well as the effects of ATP binding on the conformation of the nucleotide cleft.

claims.claim: The relative proportion of singly- versus doubly-attached states of kinesin dimers may vary depending on the kind of nucleotide analog used in the study.
claims.source: However, a recent study from Mickolajczyk et al. showed that, with ATPγS, the kinesin dimer persists in a one-head-bound state for most of the motility cycle, indicating that the relative proportion of singly- versus doubly-attached states of kinesin dimers may vary depending on the kind of nucleotide analog used in the study (Mickolajczyk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the cited study.

claims.source: Currently, it is impossible to directly correlate our experimental conditions with the aforementioned biophysical experiments, because evaporation following the final blotting step before plunge freezing of the grid can increase the concentrations of nucleotide analogs and salts in our sample to a nearly arbitrary extent, thus rendering it impossible to control for ionic strength, etc.

claims.claim: The ability to identify both two-head-bound and singly-bound dimers in the dataset indicates that there may be an equilibrium between the two states in the experimental conditions.

claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Further experiments are required to determine the significance of the equilibrium between singly- and doubly-bound states with respect to the motility cycle of kinesin.
claims.source: Further experiments are required to resolve this question and to determine the significance of such behavior with respect to the motility cycle of kinesin.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claims.claim: The undocking of the neck linker in the singly-bound head may be entropy-driven.
claims.source: The undocking of the neck linker may be entropy-driven.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of neck linker undocking.

claims.source: It is known that the thermodynamics of neck linker docking involves balance of strong opposing forces, including hydrophobic interactions between a docked neck linker and the opened docking cleft as well as high entropy gain from a disordered neck linker (Rice et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge, with citation to Rice et al., 2003.

claims.claim: In structures of monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, the neck linker is predominantly docked.
claims.source: In previous structures of monomeric kinesin with ADP•AlFx, the neck linker is predominantly docked, but in the case of a singly-bound head, a free partner head may increase the entropy gain from a disordered neck linker, favoring an undocked state (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: In the case of a singly-bound head, a free partner head may increase the entropy gain from a disordered neck linker, favoring an undocked state.

results.result: The authors developed FINDKIN, a novel cryo-EM method that combines conventional helical and single-particle approaches to locate bound kinesin motors on microtubules. FINDKIN uses a cross-correlation-based search algorithm that enumerates all possible binding patterns in overlapping search areas and applies a dual-frameset strategy (low- and high-defocus) to minimize model bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C34 collectively describe the FINDKIN methodology with clear procedural steps, validation on synthetic data (C35-C40), and strategic design choices to prevent noise bias. The method is well-documented with flowcharts and demonstrates technical innovation in addressing limitations of conventional helical reconstruction (C22-C23).

results.result: FINDKIN validation on synthetic microtubules shows false negative rates below 0.2 across all tested conditions, while false positive rates are significantly lower at high defocus (~0.2) compared to low defocus (0.4-1.2), likely due to better preservation of low-resolution signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 present systematic validation data with quantitative error rates under controlled conditions (noise, occupancy, defocus). The findings are supported by figures showing performance metrics and include mechanistic explanation for defocus-dependent performance (C39-C40).

results.result: FINDKIN enabled determination of the first structure of a two-head-bound kinesin dimer on microtubules, revealing two motor domains at sequential sites along a protofilament with resolved secondary structure at sub-nanometer resolution and coiled coil density between the heads.
results.evaluation: Claims C16 and C50-C62 describe the novel structural determination with multiple lines of evidence: resolved secondary structure (C51), coiled coil density (C54-C59), and independent validation from two binding patterns ('0110' and '011110', C61-C62). The ability to resolve secondary structure from a 20Å-filtered reference model demonstrates absence of model bias (C53).

results.result: The two-head-bound kinesin dimer structure reveals asymmetric conformations: the leading head exhibits weak nucleotide density, disordered switch I loop, undocked neck linker, and subdomain rotations (12-15° P-loop, 5-9° switch I/II), while the trailing head shows strong nucleotide density, ordered switch I loop, and docked neck linker.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C78 present multiple converging structural features distinguishing the two heads, supported by cross-correlation analysis (C63: scores 0.91-0.92 within head types vs 0.86-0.88 between types), density observations (C64-C66, C69-C72), and quantitative subdomain rotation measurements (C76-C77). The consistency across independent reconstructions strengthens the findings.

results.result: The two-head-bound structure supports the 'alternating cleft' model: the trailing head resembles ATP-like monomeric kinesin (closed nucleotide cleft, open docking cleft), while the leading head resembles no-nucleotide state (open nucleotide cleft, closed docking cleft), as confirmed by cross-correlation analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C80-C86 connect structural observations to the alternating cleft model with quantitative support from cross-correlation scores (C84-C85: trailing heads 0.73-0.74 with ATP-like vs 0.67 with apo; leading heads 0.77-0.78 with apo vs 0.69 with ATP-like). The structural features are consistent with predictions from prior monomeric studies (C73, C74).

results.result: A second population of singly-bound kinesin dimers was identified, where the attached motor domain adopts a novel conformation: ATP-like nucleotide cleft closure and ordered switch I loop, but with a disordered neck linker and no coiled coil density.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C87-C94 describe a novel structural state with clear distinguishing features. The absence of diagonal kinesin density (C88) rules out alternative stepping configurations. The structural characterization includes nucleotide cleft state (C89), switch I loop (C90), subdomain orientations matching trailing head (C91), but distinct neck linker behavior (C92-C93).

results.result: The different conformations of the two heads in the dimer arise from different neck linker orientations rather than different nucleotide conditions, providing direct evidence for neck linker-mediated allosteric coupling between the docking cleft and nucleotide cleft.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C103 present a mechanistic explanation supported by the key observation that biochemically identical heads in the same environment exhibit different conformations (C98). The logical inference that neck linker orientation is the distinguishing factor (C99) is well-supported, and the alternating cleft model provides structural explanation (C100-C102). Direct visualization of this coupling (C103) is a major advance.

results.result: Discrepancies between the dimer map and monomeric kinesin structures (residual nucleotide density in leading head, smaller P-loop rotation) may arise from either ATP binding in the leading head or contamination with singly-bound heads, with computational modeling supporting the contamination hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C116 identify important discrepancies and propose two non-mutually-exclusive explanations. While computational modeling (C112) supports the contamination artifact, the authors acknowledge that neither explanation can be definitively ruled out (C108, C116) and call for further experiments (C117). The uncertainty is appropriately recognized.

results.result: The singly-bound head structure challenges the neck linker power stroke model, suggesting that neck linker docking may be entropy-driven and weaker than in monomeric kinesin, and that full neck linker docking may not be required for ATP hydrolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C118 and C125-C134 present mechanistic interpretations of the singly-bound head structure. The evidence against the power stroke model (C130-C131) is supported by comparison with prior EPR studies and consistency with recent nanogold imaging (C132). The inference about hydrolysis not requiring full docking (C133-C134) is supported by structural observations and consistent with recent kinetic studies (C135).

results.result: The authors propose a model for the kinesin motility cycle where the two structural states (two-head-bound and singly-bound) represent consecutive states: ATP binding closes the nucleotide cleft without docking the neck linker (modeled by singly-bound head), followed by hydrolysis-accelerated neck linker docking enabling forward stepping, with inter-head tension gating ATP binding/hydrolysis in the leading head.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C147 present a mechanistic model integrating the structural findings. While the model is logical and consistent with the structures and recent kinetic studies (C140 cites Milic 2014, Mickolajczyk 2015), it remains speculative as acknowledged by the authors (C143). The model makes testable predictions but requires future structural studies with ATP for validation.

results.result: Experimental conditions used substoichiometric kinesin binding (~0.6 motor domain per tubulin dimer) to prevent oversaturation, yielding a ~5Å microtubule reconstruction. FINDKIN analysis required methodological refinements to address false negative errors and 'frame shift' contamination.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 describe experimental design and methodological problem-solving. The substoichiometric binding strategy (C41-C42) addresses limitations of prior studies. The identification of contamination issues (C45-C46) and development of solutions using dual-frameset validation (C47-C49) demonstrates rigorous methodology, though it introduces selective noise bias at vacant sites (C49).

results.result: The presence of both two-head-bound and singly-bound dimers suggests an equilibrium between these states under the experimental conditions, though the relative proportions may vary with nucleotide analog type and cannot be directly correlated with biophysical experiments due to uncontrolled evaporation during sample preparation.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124 acknowledge unexpected findings and experimental limitations. The inference of equilibrium (C123) is reasonable but the inability to control ionic strength due to evaporation (C122) prevents definitive interpretation. The authors appropriately call for further experiments (C124) to determine biological significance.

results.result: FINDKIN represents an important advance for studying heterogeneous helical polymers by enabling sorting of individual subunits into distinct structural classes, though current limitations include requirement for prior structural information and future development will incorporate likelihood/Bayesian frameworks.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C155 assess FINDKIN's broader impact and limitations. The advance over conventional methods (C150, C151-C152) is demonstrated by the successful application to kinesin dimers. The acknowledged limitations (C153-C154) and proposed future directions (C155) show appropriate self-assessment.

results.result: The results disfavor the competing 'water cap' model for inter-head coordination, which involves melting of the C-terminus of the switch II helix and other structural features not observed in the dimer map.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 presents a negative result regarding an alternative model. The inference is supported by the absence of expected structural features in the high-quality dimer map, though the evaluation is necessarily indirect.

results.result: The resolution estimates (~7Å for '010' and '0110', ~9Å for '011110') may be affected by over-refinement, as the observed secondary structure quality appears worse than expected for the reported resolutions.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 represents appropriate self-criticism about potential methodological limitations. The authors recognize the discrepancy between FSC-based resolution estimates and observed map quality, suggesting over-refinement as a probable cause and proposing future improvements.
